questions.prompt: Complete: "You ___ smoke here; it's a hospital."
questions.explanation: Nobody has the right to smoke in a hospital, so it is a prohibition: "mustn't" + base verb — you mustn't smoke here. "mustn't to" wrongly adds "to"; "can" and "might" would say that smoking is possible here, the opposite of the rule.

questions.prompt: Complete: "You ___ drink more water when it is hot."
questions.explanation: "Ought to" + base verb gives advice, and "ought" never goes without its "to": you ought to drink more water. "should" is the twin that never takes "to", so "should to" is wrong; and a modal never takes -s.

questions.prompt: Complete: "My brother ___ get up at six because his school is far."
questions.explanation: "My brother" is he, and obligation with he / she / it is "has to" + base verb: my brother has to get up at six. "have to" is for I / you / we / they, "haves" does not exist, and "has" alone loses the "to" of the obligation.

questions.prompt: Complete: "Next month my sister ___ take the national exam, so she is revising now."
questions.explanation: "Next month" is the future, and future obligation is "will have to" + base verb: she will have to take the exam. "must" has no future form, so "will must" is wrong; after "will" the verb stays bare — "have", never "has" or "having".

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence that expresses inability.

options.text: I can't swim, but my brother can.
You shouldn't swim just after a big lunch.

questions.explanation: Inability is "can't" (or "be unable to") + base verb: I can't swim — I am not able to. "Don't" and "mustn't" express prohibition (you have no right to do it), and "shouldn't" gives advice.

questions.prompt: Which word can replace "might" in "Chemicals in the river might kill the fish." without changing the meaning?
questions.explanation: "Could" is similar to "may" and "might": all three say that something is possible (perhaps). "must" would make it an obligation, "should" would turn it into advice, and "can't" would say it is impossible.
